newsitem.title: INDIA: India sets course for lower interest rates.
newsitem.headline: India sets course for lower interest rates.

text.p: India's central bank on Tuesday relaxed its credit and monetary policy in a bid to bring down interest rates of commercial banks and boost their lendable resources.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced a first-half 1997/98 (April-March) credit policy aimed at complementing a widely acclaimed pro-growth budget, which will be debated by parliament next week.
India's United Front alliance government was defeated in a confidence vote last week and negotiations were continuing on Tuesday to forge another coalition led by it.
RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said he expected interest rates to come down as a result of the policy, which also lowered interest rates on bank deposits.
"I think interest rates will come down, because the steps taken in this policy will lead to an increase in the lendable resources of banks," he told Reuters Television in an interview.
The lowest prime lending rate among India's major banks is 14.5 percent.

"We have also lowered deposit rates which should get reflected in lower lending rates," Rangarajan said. "The full impact of the reduction in cash reserve ratios made last year will be felt this year. This will also help."
The central bank reduced the ceiling on interest on deposits of up to one year by one percentage point to give banks more leeway to cut lending rates.
The RBI said the maximum interest rate on deposits up to one year was being cut to 9.0 percent a year from 10 percent.
Rangarajan said a number of steps had been taken in the credit policy to improve the credit delivery system.
"I think the credit delivery system has to improve and we have taken a number of steps in the credit policy to improve it," he said.
"We have given greater autonomy to banks to determine working capital limits for borrowers and also eased norms on consortium lending," he said.
Rangarajan said the capital market would be boosted by credit policy announcements allowing banks to invest more in shares of companies.

The RBI also said it was removing reserve requirements on inter-bank borrowings. Banks in India now avoid borrowing on their fortnightly reporting day as borrowings on the reporting day attracts reserve requirements.
The move is expected to pave the way for the creation of an interbank term lending market.
